name: Lake Miwok

catalog_citation: Callaghan, Catherine A. 1963. A Grammar of the Lake Miwok Language. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley (UMI scan, eScholarship qt9hr2605b).
catalog_quote: There are two degrees of phonemic stress in Lake Miwok, /ˊ/ and no mark. ... /ˊ/ is emphasis and falling pitch [ˆ] on long final syllables and occasionally on long open pre-final syllables. Otherwise, /ˊ/ is emphasis and high pitch [ˊ]. The last stressed syllable in a sentence tends to have a higher pitch than preceding stressed syllables. [p. 40] ... Morphophonemic stress shift is obligatory across morpheme boundaries and optional across word boundaries. It can be schematized as follows: //CV́C(h)V(V)CV// = /CVC(h)V́VCV/ //CV́C(h)VCCV// = /CVC(h)V́(V)CCV/, with /CVC(h)V́CCV/ being the commoner alternant. [p. 50] ... There are both stressed and unstressed roots, but affixes never bear the stress. ... A WORD comprises one or more roots with accompanying affixes. Only one of these roots may be a stressed root, although not all words contain a stressed root. [p. 53]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Re-read the three quoted passages on the 300-dpi page images and on a fresh render of PDF p. 59 (book p. 53). All quoted sentences are there verbatim: p. 40 sec. 150 "There are two degrees of phonemic stress in Lake Miwok, /'/ and no mark."; sec. 151 "/'/ is emphasis and falling pitch [^] on long final syllables and occasionally on long open pre-final syllables. Otherwise, /'/ is emphasis and high pitch ['].. It is assumed that these examples were followed by final juncture."; p. 50 sec. 182.6 "Morphophonemic stress shift is obligatory across morpheme boundaries and optional across word boundaries.[fn 2: This criterion defines the word boundary.] It can be schematized as follows: //CV'C(h)V…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is contrastive and lexically tied to the root: roots are either stressed ('strong') or unstressed ('weak'), affixes never carry stress, and a word has at most one stressed root. In root citation forms the stress sits on the first syllable (páawih 'mountain', táwhal 'work', kíik 'water', káluk 'skunk'), but an obligatory morphophonemic rule moves it to the second syllable, lengthening that vowel if the syllable is open, whenever the word has the shape CV.CV(V).CV or CV.CVC.CV: //táwhal-ṭak// -> tawháalak 'worker', //ˀúpuh-ṭak// -> ˀupúutak 'swimmer', //káni-ni// -> kaníini 'with me', //hówo-nˀi// -> howónni 'chair', //ˀúte-po// -> ˀutéppo. Roots whose first syllable is heavy (CVC or CVV) keep initial stress (jólkati, tállahmi, kaˀáppi). My inference from her schema and examples (not her wording): surface stress is initial when the first syllable is heavy or the word is disyllabic, otherwise on the second syllable — effectively a weight-sensitive pattern packaged as root stress plus a shift rule. Stressed syllables carry high pitch, falling pitch on long final syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; only two degrees (/ˊ/ versus no mark). §152: unmarked syllables have lower pitch and less emphasis, and non-final short open unstressed syllables are shortest and weakest of all.
new_statements.exceptions: Unstressed words exist (particles, weak roots) and 'not all words contain a stressed root'. Roots with a heavy first syllable keep initial stress (jólkati, pítkati, tállahmi, ˀáppi). Across word boundaries the shift is optional. Note: p. 51 opens 'Elsewhere, there is no stress shift, e.g.,' but most of the examples that follow (tawháalak, ˀupúutak, kaníini, keˀéeti) do show the shift; the layout of the typescript is ambiguous there.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonemic stress (one stressed root per word; some words, e.g. particles and weak roots, carry no stress). The p. 40 examples are stated to be 'followed by final juncture', i.e. citation/isolation forms; the pitch remarks are sentence-level. Stress shift is obligatory inside the word and optional across word boundaries in phrases (kawá(a)j kaˀúte ~ káwaj kaˀúte 'I see the horse').
new_statements.identity_note: Lake Miwok proper (lake1258), the single language of the Clear Lake / Middletown area; Callaghan's 1963 data come from the last eight or so speakers on the Middletown Rancheria in the late 1950s. No dialect subdivision is described.

sources.note: Sec. 150-152 (p. 40): two degrees of phonemic stress, /ˊ/ vs no mark; /ˊ/ = emphasis + high pitch, falling pitch on long final syllables; last stressed syllable of a sentence highest. Sec. 210-211 (p. 53): roots are stressed or unstressed, affixes never bear stress, a word has at most one stressed root. Sec. 182.6 (pp. 50-51): obligatory morphophonemic stress shift //CV́C(h)V(V)CV// -> /CVC(h)V́VCV/, //CV́C(h)VCCV// -> /CVC(h)V́(V)CCV/ across morpheme boundaries, optional across word boundaries (tawháalak 'worker', ˀupúutak 'swimmer', howónni 'chair').
Phonology section gives vowel and consonant inventories only; nothing on stress. Its reference list supplied the eScholarship link to Callaghan 1963 that made the dissertation fetchable.
